q: What are the main Chinese creation myths?
Who are the Eight Immortals in Chinese mythology?
What is the role of dragons in Chinese mythology?
a: Chinese mythology is rich with creation myths, the most famous being Pangu, who emerged from a cosmic egg and separated yin from yang, creating heaven and earth, with his body parts transforming into the natural world after his death. The Eight Immortals (Ba Xian) are legendary Taoist figures — including Lu Dongbin, Li Tieguai, and He Xiangu — who gained immortality through their virtues and studies, each possessing a magical power and object, and they feature widely in folk tales and art. The Monkey King (Sun Wukong) is the central character of the classic novel Journey to the West, a trickster deity born from stone who gains supernatural powers, rebels against heaven, and later accompanies the monk Xuanzang on a pilgrimage to India. Chinese dragons (long) are benevolent, wise creatures associated with water, rain, and imperial power, unlike the fire-breathing dragons of Western mythology.

q: What is Shinto in Japanese mythology?
a: Japanese mythology is deeply rooted in Shinto, the indigenous spiritual tradition centered on kami — divine spirits or forces inhabiting natural elements like trees, rivers, mountains, and ancestors. The creation myth begins with Izanagi and Izanami, divine siblings who churned the primordial ocean with a jeweled spear to create the Japanese islands, but their union also produced numerous kami until Izanami died giving birth to the fire god. Amaterasu, the sun goddess and ruler of the heavenly realm Takamagahara, is considered the ancestress of the Japanese imperial family, and famously hid in a cave plunging the world into darkness until the other gods lured her out with a mirror and dance. Susanoo, her tempestuous brother, is the god of storms and the sea who slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi and later repented his violent behavior. Yokai are a vast category of supernatural creatures, ghosts, and spirits in Japanese folklore, ranging from mischievous (like the shape-shifting kitsune foxes) to terrifying (like the vengeful onryo), and remain hugely popular in modern anime, manga, and film.

q: What are the main myths of Korea?
What are the myths of Southeast Asia?
What are the myths of Central Asia?
What is the Vietnamese creation myth?
a: Korean mythology centers on Dangun, the legendary founder of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, born from a bear woman (who became human after enduring a 100-day ordeal in a cave) and the son of the heavenly god Hwanung. Southeast Asian myths are diverse, with Vietnamese mythology featuring the dragon lord Lac Long Quan and the fairy Au Co, whose hundred children became the ancestors of the Vietnamese people, and Thai mythology incorporating Hindu influences with the god Indra and the serpent Naga. Central Asian mythology features Turkic and Mongol traditions including the legend of Ergenekon (a mythical valley where a she-wolf guided the Turks to freedom), Tengri (the sky god), and shamanic epic traditions like the Manas epic of the Kyrgyz people.

q: What are the main myths of India?
Who is Vishnu in Hindu mythology?
What is the churning of the ocean?
a: Indian mythology, primarily recorded in Hindu scriptures, features a vast pantheon with the Trimurti of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver), and Shiva (destroyer). Vishnu is known for his ten avatars (dashavatara), including Rama (hero of the Ramayana), Krishna (central figure of the Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita), and the yet-to-come Kalki. The Ramayana tells the story of Prince Rama's quest to rescue his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana with the help of the monkey god Hanuman. The Mahabharata, one of the longest epic poems in the world, recounts the Kurukshetra War between the Pandavas and Kauravas and contains the Bhagavad Gita, a foundational philosophical text. The churning of the ocean (Samudra Manthana) describes how gods and demons worked together to churn the cosmic ocean, producing the elixir of immortality along with numerous treasures and threats.
